entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Verrius Flaccus was a Roman grammarian and teacher who flourished under Augustus and Tiberius.

Born in Rome around 70 BCE, Flaccus rose to prominence as a skilled orator and linguist, becoming a favorite among the Roman elite.

His most significant contribution was the codification of Latin grammar, as outlined in his work "Adversaria," which became a standard reference for Latin scholars.

Flaccus's influence extended beyond the realm of language, as his expertise in rhetoric and eloquence made him a sought-after advisor to prominent Roman leaders.

Despite his enduring legacy, Flaccus's life remains somewhat of a mystery, with few records of his personal life or family.

As a testament to his enduring impact, Flaccus's work continues to be studied and revered by scholars today.

In the annals of Roman history, Flaccus's name serves as a reminder of the power of language and learning to shape the course of human civilization.
